doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Krupa as mentor, lessons in New York and Ed Shaughnessy
summary: Krupa makes Igoe his protege and sends him to a New York teacher; he befriends Ed Shaughnessy and says reputation ended auditions after Goodman.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: And I was a lucky kid. I was lucky I met those guys, and had that opportunity to play with them at an early age, and I was a heavy listener and a heavy practicer. And I had some luck. And that was a lucky day for me because I was a little on the sick side, I had a sore throat and a little temperature. They said, “maybe you better stay home.” I said, “no I’m not going to stay home, take me down there.” Because I couldn’t drive. So that was it. And Gene kind of adopted me as his protégé. I’d go see him play at different places and he’d “come on up here.” And he’d be signing autographs. And people went, “who’s that kid? Who’s that kid?” And he said, “this is my protégé. Sonny Igoe, and he’s a protégé of mine.” Because he sent me to a teacher in New York after I won the contest. My mother said to him, “do you think he can do anything with the drums?” He said, “are you kidding? He can’t miss.” So he said, “I have a teacher for you to go to in New York.” She said, “New York?” So she took me to the first lesson. And then I went by myself. At that time from Ridgewood to New York the bus fare was 35 cents. So I used to go for my lessons in New York and come home on my own. I was 16. And it was a marvelous time for me. But then I was into the mix in New York already. Competition with other students who were coming in to this guy and they were hanging around and talking and this, that and the other thing.

A very famous drummer, he and I became very good friends over the years, Ed Shaughnessy. And he took lessons with the same guy. And we were sort of like, as we got older, friendly rivals. And I went in the service and Ed was too young. And when I came out he was still there. And so we took up our friendship again. And we were helpful to each other in our careers. And I recommended him for jobs and he recommended me. Because you can’t do anything alone in this business. You’ve got to have help. I had a lot of help when I was a kid, you know people telling me things, giving me advice. And you can’t do anything without people recommending you. Your reputation precedes you, and when you’ve done a certain amount of things with a certain amount of people, then you don’t audition anymore. The thing with me was when I got the gig with Benny Goodman and played with him for a year, after that I didn’t have to audition for anybody. They’d just call and say are you available. Because they figured if I could play with Benny, that’s a good test.
So that was after the war though. The other things were pre-war.
